questions.title: Apply a Discount Using a Lambda
questions.module: Module 15: Lambdas, Functional Interfaces, and Streams
questions.objective: Declare a functional interface and implement it with a lambda.
questions.problem_statement:
Create a functional interface PriceOperation with a method double apply(double price). Read a whole-number price in rupees and a whole-number discount percentage. Create a lambda that calculates the discounted price using price * (100 - discount) / 100.0.

For this problem, all input prices and percentages are integers, so the input has no fractional-cent rounding ambiguity. Print the final price with exactly two decimal places using Locale.US.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes and interfaces without the public keyword.

Explanation: A 15% discount on 1000 is 150, leaving a final price of 850.00.
questions.input_format:
First line: integer price.
Second line: integer discount percentage.
questions.output_format: Print Final price: <price> with two digits after the decimal point.
questions.constraints:
0 ≤ price ≤ 1,000,000
0 ≤ discount percentage ≤ 100
hints: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method; @FunctionalInterface documents that.
The lambda can use the discount variable from main, because it is effectively final.
Format with String.format(Locale.US, "%.2f", result).

questions.title: Build a Top-K Product Report
questions.module: Module 15: Lambdas, Functional Interfaces, and Streams
questions.objective: Aggregate with groupingBy and summingLong, then rank with a two-key comparator and limit().
questions.problem_statement:
An online store receives sales records containing a product name and the number of units sold. Multiple records may refer to the same product. Calculate total units sold per product using Collectors.groupingBy() with a summing collector.

Rank products by total units sold in descending order. If totals are equal, order products by name in ascending lexicographical order. Use Comparator.comparing() and thenComparing() to express the ordering rules. Return at most K products; if fewer than K distinct products exist, print all available products.

Use long for aggregated quantities. Product names are single tokens.

Required technique: Use a grouping collector, a summing operation, and Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...).

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes and interfaces without the public keyword.

Explanation: The totals are Mouse = 30, Keyboard = 20, Monitor = 15, and Cable = 3. The first three products are selected by descending total. When totals tie, the product name determines the order.
questions.input_format:
First line: integers N and K.
Next N lines: product name and quantity sold.
questions.output_format:
Print one line per selected product:
<product>: <totalQuantity>
questions.constraints:
1 ≤ N ≤ 100,000
1 ≤ K ≤ 100,000
0 ≤ quantity sold ≤ 1,000,000,000
Product names contain 1–100 characters.
Each product's total fits in a Java long.
sample_inputs:
6 3
Mouse 10
Keyboard 15
Mouse 20
Monitor 15
Keyboard 5
Cable 3
hints: groupingBy(r -> r[0], Collectors.summingLong(r -> Long.parseLong(r[1]))) gives a Map<String, Long>.
Java often can't infer the entry type for a chained comparator; declaring Comparator<Map.Entry<String, Long>> byTotal = Comparator.comparing(Map.Entry::getValue); first helps.
Sort the entry stream with byTotal.reversed().thenComparing(Map.Entry::getKey), then call limit(k).
